Abstract
In this study, a high dimensional neural network potential for the smectite pyro-
phyllite clay has been developped from DFT data including correction for dispersion
interactions. The dataset has been built from the adaptive learning approach, resulting
in a diverse and very concise set of selected structures comprising only representative
ones. Two NNP datasets have been constituted from sets of energies and forces com-
puted at two different levels of DFT accuracy. Validation tests show very good accuracy
for the computed energies and forces of various systems differing by their size and simu-
lation conditions. The developed potentials are able to reproduce structural parameters
with excellent agreement with DFT values as well as experimental data, and are the
first NNPS able to reproduce clay layers’ properties held together via van der Waals
interactions. The NNP constructed from data of higher DFT level show better results
for extreme condition simulations. In addition, elastic properties, exfoliation energies
and vibrational density of state are also well reproduced showing better performances
than standard force fields at a fraction of DFT computation time.

1
Introduction
Clay phyllosilicate minerals are naturally abundant in Nature.
Their large surface area
and layered structure give them unique physical and chemical properties such as ionic ex-
change, swelling, and adsorption properties.1 Thus, they are used in various applications,
such as catalysis,2–4 and notably for environmental decontamination.5,6 Different families of
clay minerals are categorized according to the organization of their tetrahedral layers and
octahedral layers as well as the nature and amount of isomorphic substitutions.7 Pyrophyl-
lite: Al2(Si4O10)(OH)2, is one of the simplest dioctahedral phyllosilicate (two-thirds of the
octahedral sites occupied) with two SiO4 tetrahedral (T) sheets sandwiching one Al2O3 oc-
tahedral (O) sheet (see Figure 1). The different TOT sheets are covalently bonded forming
one layer, while the layers are held together through van der Waals bonding.
Contrary
to other clay minerals, pyrophyllite does not have any substitution in the T or O sheets
and thus does not carry a permanent charge. Due to their great adsorption capacity, py-
rophyllite clays can have applications in the treatment of pollutants, e.g. for removal of
organic compounds like methylene blue8 and more recently for removal of nitrate from soil
and artificial fertilizers.9 To study pyrophyllite clay properties, in addition to experimental
studies, theoretical approaches may provide insight on structural, electronic, and dynamical
properties.10 Atomistic simulations allow to explore a system potential energy surface (PES)
to access thermodynamic, vibrational, and mechanical properties.11,12 Molecular dynamics
(MD) simulations were used to investigate pyrophyllite adsorption performances for a wide
range of compounds: metal cations such as cesium,13 aqueous uranyl (IV),14 methane,15
nitric acid and nitrogen dioxide,16 CO2,17 etc. The generally applied parametrized force
fields are dedicated to a given family of compounds such as organics, biomolecules, minerals,
etc. Various force fields were developed specifically for clays minerals such as ClayFF18 or
polarized force fields (PIM).19,20 Other more general force fields such as the INTERFACE
FF21 parametrized on inorganic surfaces interacting with organic, and biomolecules (using
adjusted parameters of bio-organics existing force fields) or ReaxFF22 developed for reactive
2


events at the solid-liquid-gaz interfaces are also used for clay minerals studies. These meth-
ods enable large-scale simulations, but their accuracy depends on their specificity, resulting
in non-negligible approximation when mixing with other force fields (i.e. for interaction of
clays with organic compounds).
On the other hand, more portable and accurate electronic structure methods such as
density functional theory (DFT) allows carrying out high-level ab initio MD (AIMD).23
While DFT computations give accurate PES, very high computational costs and resources
are needed, which brings narrow limitations to the time and spatial scale of the simulations.
New methods overcoming these limitations are emerging based on approximated potential
energy surfaces (PES) fitted to DFT’s ones through machine learning approaches. These
approximated PESs can then be used to run large-scale MD simulations with DFT-level
accuracy, allowing simulation of reactive processes. A popular way is the method proposed
by Behler and Parinello24 using high-dimensional neural networks trained on ab initio data.
Recently, such neural network potentials (NNP) were successfully constructed for kaolinite,
a TO dioctahedral clay whose layers are held through hydrogen bonding.
Kobayashi et
al. created NNPs based on DFT training data produced with different functionals: PBE
and SCAN.25 They noted a better performance of the NNP fitted on SCAN data than
the NNP fitted on PBE data especially when dispersion corrections were not taken into
account on the PBE calculations. Sheperd et al. produced NNPs based on DFT data with a
revPBE functional26 with either Grimme’s D3 correction or Dion’s correction. They noted
that the NNPs fitted on revPBE-Dion reproduced more accurately structural properties of
the material while the NNPs fitted on revPBE-D3 predicted vibrational properties closer
to the experiments. All in all, the created NNPs were able to reproduce quite accurately
structural, mechanical and vibrational properties of kaolinites at a low computational cost.
In the present study, we also applied the Behler-Parinello method to create an NNP for
pyrophyllite as a model for TOT smectite clays, which layers interact via van der Waals
interactions. Pyrophyllite was chosen as a first simple model, with the perspective of extend
3


later the dataset for substituted and hydrated clays. The NNP was trained on data from
DFT with the PBE-D3 functional.
A well-built dataset is a crucial part of creating an
accurate NNP. A smart approach to build a comprehensive, concise, and diverse dataset is
to use an adaptive learning (or active learning) scheme.27,28 This iterative scheme using the
discrepancy of predicted quantities (energy and forces) between test-NNPs allows selecting
and adding representative structures to the dataset.
2
Methodology
2.1
Pyrophyllite model
Figure 1: 2 × 1 × 1 pyrophyllite supercell (80 atoms) with tetrahedral and octahedral sites:
Oa apical oxygen, Ob basal oxygen, Oh oxygen of hydroxil group. d001 represents the basal
spacing.
The pyrophyllite triclinic unit cell determined by Lee and Guggenheim29 was used:
5.160 × 8.966 × 9.347 ˚A3 with α = 91.180◦, β = 100.460◦, and γ = 89.640◦. As a database
starting point, the unit cell was replicated in the x direction to create 2×1×1 supercells (see
Figure 1) containing 80 atoms. In addition, orthorhombic cells were also used. As compared
to the triclinic cell, the orthorhombic cell will have an effect on the sliding between layers,
4


which is often observed at room temperature. Moreover, the orthorhombic cell is widely
used in simulations with smectite clays comprising water and cations in the interlayer space.
2.2
NNP
The NNPs were build using the n2p2 software.30 The neural network used for the final
training had two hidden layers of 25 nodes each. The softplus and linear activation functions
for the hidden and output layers have been used, respectively. The loss function used was the
root-mean squared error (RMSE). In the Behler-Parinello method, the descriptor is given in
the form of atom centered symmetry functions,31,32 which are many-body functions damped
by a cutoff function with cutoff radius set at 6 ˚A. For each set of radial symmetry functions,
two functions were defined with the shifted radius rs kept at 0.0, two with rs shifted according
to the distance of the first neighbor and two with rs shifted according to the distance of the
second neighbor (see the SI for more details). The distances were taken from an equilibrium
structure. Four angular functions were defined for each angle between covalently bonded
atoms types. For the training process, the dataset is splited into two subsets; 90% goes to
the training set and 10% goes to the test set.
2.3
Dataset generation
The accuracy of an NNP is greatly dependent on the dataset used for the training. The
dataset should well represent the system of interest while avoiding over-representation of
particular configurations. Diverse structures covering all relevant configurations should be
included, otherwise the NNP will have poor extrapolation capacity. On the other hand,
too many similar configurations might result in overfitting due to the high flexibility and
nonphysical nature of the NNP – the non-occurence of overfitting was checked by ensuring
that the loss on the training and validation set do not diverge from each other. As such,
building the training dataset is a key point in the development of an NNP.
5


2.3.1
Adaptive learning
The scheme used was already successfully applied in a previous work,33 and it is extensively
described there. The advantage of the adaptive learning procedure is to enrich the dataset
iteratively from two phases: the adaptive and the renewal (see Figure 2). The former allows
the selection of representative structures from a stock library to improve the dataset repre-
sentativity. The latter starts with extreme conditions MDs allowing to explore rare events
and directly selects these rare events structures (“extrapolation warning”, EW structures);
it is followed by the generation of new structures (made from random moves of atoms from
these EW structures) that will allow to enrich the stock library for the next iteration. As
such, only structures selected to enter the dataset are computed via DFT. For the adap-
tive phase, we generated two intermediate NNPs differing by the number of nodes in the
hidden layers: 15–15 and 20–20. These two NNPs were used to predict the energies of a
stock library. At each iteration, the 50 structures with the largest energy difference between
the two NNPs were computed with DFT and added to the dataset. When the convergence
criteria was reached, i.e. when the difference between energies computed with the two NNPs
averaged on the stock library converged, the resulting dataset was used to train a final NNP.
The resulting NNP was then used in the renewal phase to conduct test MDs on the 2×1×1
supercells in NVT and NPT ensembles at 300 K, 500 K and 1000 K, with temperature ramps
of 100,000 steps between production runs.
For each symmetry function the range of values present in the dataset was computed,
allowing easy identification of extrapolation cases during molecular dynamics, i.e. cases where
the structures explored were not represented in the dataset. If there were such structures
generating extrapolation warnings (EW structures) during the test MDs, single point DFT
calculations were systematically performed on the structures, and they were added to the
dataset. Random atom displacements and constraints were also applied to those structures
to extend the stock library. In all cases, the structures were added to the dataset if all
individual forces components were under the threshold value of 25 eV/˚A. This adaptive

2.3.2
Stock library generation
To generate the initial stock library, standard AIMD simulations were run in the NVE
ensemble on the 2×1×1 pyrophyllite supercells at 300 K, 500 K and 1000 K as described in
section 2.4.1. Triclinic and orthorhombic supercells were created with varying basal spacing
(d001) from 9.0 to 9.5 ˚A with a step size of 0.1 ˚A. In order to explore out of equilibrium
structures, constrained AIMD at 300 K were carried out with the triclinic and orthorhombic
supercells with d001 = 9.0 ˚A. The constraints consisted of lattice vectors a and b scaling of
7


±10%, cell angles tilt of ±10%, and lattice isotropic strain of ±10%. To correctly describe the
OH bonds, less represented in the pyrophyllite cell containing only four of them, structures
with OH bond length modified between 0.7 ˚A to 1.4 ˚A were added to the stock. For the
same purpose, structures with water in the interlayer and c lattice vector increased to 22 ˚A
were optimized by doing classical MD in the NPT ensemble before running AIMD at 300 K,
500 K and 1000 K and added to the stock. These structures, containing between 80 and 200
atoms, constituted the initial stock library starting the adaptive learning procedure.
2.4
Atomistic calculations
Classical molecular dynamics were performed using the LAMMPS software,34 either using
the LAMMPS NNP package35 or the ClayFF force fields.18
2.4.1
DFT
The Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP)36 was used to perform plane wave periodic
DFT calculations. The exchange-correlation energy was described with the PBE functional37
in the frame of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA). The DFT-D3 Grimme cor-
rection38 was used to describe the van der Waals interaction. Projected augmented waves39
were used to describe the ionic cores and the valence electrons were described with planes-
wave basis sets. The sampling of the Brillouin zone was made only at the Γ-point (following
the Monkhorst-Pack method). The calculations were performed with a kinetic energy cut-off
of 400 eV. During structure geometry optimization calculation the threshold for the force
convergence was set to 0.01 eV/˚A. The productions were usually run for 2 ps. As plane-waves
were used, discontinuity in the plane waves basis set can occur when the shape or size of
the box change during simulation. So only for the NPT simulations, the energy cutoff was
increased to 600 eV to saturate the plane wave basis set so that it will not lose accuracy
when the size of the box change during simulation.
8


2.4.2
NNPs validation
Once the dataset was constructed, to validate the final trained NNPs, we compared the
forces and energies obtained from AIMD with those computed by the developed NNPs for
each structure of the trajectory. The AIMD was performed on a 2 × 1 × 2 supercell with
2 layers (configuration not included in the dataset). The dynamics were run in the NVE
ensemble following the procedure described in 2.4.1. For each step, the corresponding struc-
ture was extracted, the energy as well as the forces on the atoms were computed using the
NNPs. The NNPs and DFT energies were then plotted for each step of the MD. For the
forces, random atoms among important atom types (surface, internal and hydroxil oxygen,
hydrogen, silicium, and aluminium) were chosen and the individual forces component and
norm of the forces acting on these atoms were plotted.
2.4.3
Energetic profile of the d001
For validation purposes, the profile of the energy evolution according to the basal spacing
was investigated. The basal spacing can be determined experimentally using XRD by the
position of the (001) ray so it will also be called d001 in the following. Supercells with different
d001 were created from a triclinic 2 × 1 × 1 supercell by varying the c lattice vector to get
the corresponding d001 according to the formula d001 = c × sinβ. Fourteen supercells with a
d001 ranging from 8.95 to 9.60 ˚A with a step size of 0.05 ˚A were constructed. The position
of the ions on these supercells was optimized at the DFT level.
Classical MDs in the NVT ensemble at 300 K were performed with the NNPs or ClayFF
starting from the optimized supercells. In this case, the thermalization was performed in
two runs (see SI for details). For comparison with the developed NNPs, AIMDs were also
performed in the NVT ensemble at 300 K (cut-off energy: 400 eV). To plot the energy profile,
the total energy was averaged for each production run to obtain an average energy per d001
for the NNPs, ClayFF, and DFT.
9


2.4.4
Structural parameters
The lattice parameters were studied with the developed NNPs on different supercells and
compared with the experimental results, DFT and ClayFF. Simulations were performed in
the NPT ensemble to follow the evolution of the lattice parameters. The productions for
classical MD, with ClayFF or the NNPs, were run in the NPT ensemble for 500 ps. AIMD
with an energy cut-off of 600 eV were run in the NPT ensemble for 2 ps at 300 K. The
different lattice parameters were calculated by averaging over the production runs. The error
was calculated with respect to the DFT values. In addition, unit cell and ionic positions
relaxation was also performed using the NNPs, ClayFF and DFT. In this case, the error
was calculated with respect to the experimental values given by Lee and Guggenheim.29 To
obtain the radial distribution functions, MDs were performed in the NVE ensemble on the
4 × 2 × 1 supercell.
2.4.5
Elasticity
The elastic constant matrix Cij was calculated at 0 GPa on the triclinic unit cell with
LAMMPS by measuring the stress tensor changes after deformation of the cell. The Voigt-
Reuss-Hill approximation40 was used to calculate the bulk, shear, and elastic moduli of the
pyrophyllite, as well as the Poisson’s ratio.
2.4.6
Exfoliation energy
The exfoliation energy, the energy required to peel off a single layer of a bulk structure, was
computed by taking the difference between the unit cell energy of the bulk and that of a
single layer.41,42
Eexfo = Ebulk −Elayer,
(1)
where Ebulk is the energy off the optimized bulk configuration and Elayer is the energy of
the optimized single layer configuration.
To find the c lattice vector of the single layer
10


configuration, the c parameter was increased and the structure relaxed until the energy
converges to a plateau. Since the cut-off used for the NNPs descriptor was 6 ˚A the scan
of the c distance was started at 12 ˚A (plot available in SI). The exfoliation energy was
calculated for a c lattice vector equal to 25 ˚Afor which the DFT energy remains constant.
2.4.7
Vibrational analysis
The vibrational density of state (VDoS) was evaluated from the Fourier transfrom of the
velocity autocorrelation function obtained from NVE simulations of 10 ps at 300 K with a
timestep of 1 fs on a 4 × 2 × 1 supercell.
3
Results and discussion
3.1
Dataset construction
The process was started with a dataset of 1,000 structures taken randomly from MD simu-
lations at 300 K on the supercell with d001 = 9.0 ˚A. The initial stock library was constituted
by about 200 000 structures obtained from applied constraints as described in section 2.3.2.
The adaptive learning process was finished after two cycles. After the first cycle, a dataset
of 5,509 structures was constituted, picked from a stock library of 191,988 structures. A
final NNP with 2 hidden layers of 25 nodes was trained on 300 epochs. The obtained RMSE
values on the test set are 1.2 meV/atom for the energy and 164.9 meV/˚A for the forces.
However the MD tests did not arrive to completion, i.e. 400 structures with extrapolation
warning were raised and then calculated by single point DFT and added to the dataset.
Constraints of ±5% on cell vectors and angles as well as random atom displacement of 0.1 ˚A
were applied to these structures, hence 42,839 structures were added directly to the stock
library.
After the second cycle of adaptive learning, the selected dataset consisted of 6,974 struc-
tures. For kaolinite clays, Kobayashi et al. did not use dataset building scheme and had a
11


dataset of more than 20,000 structures - which is around three times our dataset. Sheperd
et al. used a scheme similar to adaptive learning and ended up with a dataset of 7,748
structures which is comparable to our final dataset size.
The final NNP (NNP400) was trained for 300 epochs. RMSE convergence was checked
for both forces and energies (see SI Figure. S1) and the best weights were taken along these
curves. A second NNP (NNP600) was created from the final dataset by recalculating the
forces and energy of each structures of the dataset at higher DFT level, with an energy
cutoff increased to 600 eV in order to better represent the change of volume in NPT sim-
ulations (see section 2.4.1). Except the level of accuracy of the DFT computation, both
NNPs followed the exact same training procedure have been trained from the same dataset
(comprising 6974 structures, with randomly chosen 90% used for the training and 10% for
the validation).

The training’s RMSE values are gathered in Table 1. There is no notable difference in
RMSE values between the two NNPs. They are also comparable to commonly accepted
RMSE values for this type of NNP typically less than 6 meV/atom for the energy and less
than 200 meV/˚A for the forces.43–46 The values obtained by Kobayashi et al. for kaolinite
clay, a similar system, are: 1.5–1.7 meV/atom for the energy and 58–68 meV/˚A for the
forces. Our NNPs have smaller errors on the energy by around 1 meV/aom. The RMSE
values on the forces for both our NNPs are around 180 meV/˚A which is acceptable although
on the higher end. These large values are due to the presence of more distorted structures
in the dataset. In fact, an increased RMSE following an adaptive learning procedure is a
12


known and expected phenomenon:27,33 the selected structures are generally non-equilibrium
ones. This allows increasing the feature space of the descriptor, reducing the risk of extrap-
olation and representing an extended PES with a still acceptable accuracy - while including
structures with high energies and forces for which a small error results in a large contribution
to the RMSE. Overall, the RMSE values on the training and testing sets are close, which
signals a good completion of the training without overfitting.

3.2
Validation
To validate the final NNPs, energies and forces of each structure of an NVE AIMD of 2 ps
trajectory at 300 K are compared to those computed with the NNPs as described in section
2.4.2. RMSE values are computed with respect to DFT calculations performed with a cut-
off of 400 eV, since that corresponds to the standard settings of VASP calculations. Both
the NNP400 and the NNP600 reproduce very well the energy variations observed during the
13


AIMD simulation as can be seen in Figure 3. The energy RMSE values are respectively
0.455 meV/atom and 0.491 meV/atom showing very good agreement between the DFT and
the NNPs. No differences in accuracy for the energy between the two NNPs was noticed.
The RMSE values obtained here are smaller than during the training. That is because in MD
trajectories the equilibrium structures are highly correlated whereas in the training dataset
the selected structures are generally out of equilibrium and decorrelated.

Exploitation

Basal Spacing

suring the basal spacing of the structure, so reproducing it through theoretical simulations
accurately is valuable.

In addition, the basal spacing d001 was computed for different supercells at different tem-
peratures from averaged values over NPT trajectories (see Table 2). The obtained d001 values
found by the NNPs are slightly overestimated by 0.15 ˚A for the unit cell at 300 K compared
to the DFT, but remains in an acceptable range of error. At 300 K the different approaches
show no size effects. Size effects start to appear at 500 K, and the NNPs overestimation
increases up to 0.25 ˚A for the unit cell, while it remains at 0.9–0.10 ˚A for larger cells. Then
the size effects become larger at 1000 K with differences up to 0.7 ˚A for the d001 calculated
with the NNP400 vs. DFT. The error in the d001 estimate decreases with increasing cell size,
the overestimation of the NNP400 compared to DFT is 0.6˚A for the unit cell at 1000 K,
16


while it is only 0.25 ˚A for the 2 × 1 × 2 supercell. However, ClayFF and the NNP600 give
stable results even at 1000 K with a smaller overestimation around 0.1–0.3 ˚A. Hence, it
seems that the NNP600 allows better description of the system when NPT simulations at
high temperature are performed, i.e. with large volume fluctuations. This was the purpose
of constructing such NNP (through higher energy cutoff DFT calculations) resulting in more
accurate energy and forces less sensible to volume variations.

The computed vibrational density of state from NNPs show a rather good agreement with
the experimental spectra or that computed with DFT, as compared to ClayFF(see Figure 10).
Experimentally, naturally occuring pyrophyllites are characterized by the presence of a peak
at 3675 cm−1 and a band at 950 cm−1 corresponding to the OH stretching and OH bending,
24


respectively.54 From the DFT calculation, the OH bending gave rise to a sharp peak at
950 cm−1. The position of this peak is shifted for NNP400 and NNP600 who display a low
intensity, broader peak at 920 cm−1, while ClayFF doesn’t reproduce this behavior. Both
NNPs show two peaks in the 1000–1200 cm−1 region; one at 1030 cm−1 and the other at
1085 cm−1 corresponding to Si-O vibrations. With the DFT calculation, the Si-O vibration
peak is much less intense and located at 1020 cm−1. As for the experimental spectra, it
shows an intense peak at 1045 cm−1 and a less intense peak at 1120 cm−1 for the Si-O
vibrations. The OH stretching peak is present for all the methods with a similar shift of
around 100 cm−1 compared to experimental results. In the 3600–4000 cm−1 where the OH
stretching band is located, both DFT, NNP400 and NNP600 show two peaks. The two DFT
peaks are sharper than the NNPs’one and are located at 3795 cm−1 and 3805 cm−1. NNP400
shows broader peaks, one located at 3775 cm−1 and the other at 3810 cm−1 while NNP600
show a slight shift with peaks at 3800 cm−1 and 3855 cm−1. The partial VDoS per atom
are available in the Supporting Information (Figure. S5). One should note that the ClayFF
force field was not parametrized on spectroscopic data which explains its lacking description
of the spectra.
4
Conclusion
In this study, NNPs for pyrophyllite clay were trained on DFT data calculated with PBE-D3
functional. Adaptive learning was used as a smart approach to construct a comprehensive,
concise, and diverse training dataset. The resulting training dataset was quite small, with
6,974 structures. Two NNPs were created: one fitted on DFT data with an energy cutoff
of 400 eV, NNP400, and the other one fitted on DFT data with an energy cutoff of 600 eV,
NNP600. The resulting NNPs are able to reproduce closely DFT energies and forces, as well
as experimental structural parameters. The constructed NNPs show very goood results in
comparison to the widely used ClayFF force field. The NNPs even show better results for
25


the d001 energy profile and the values obtained from NPT simulations at high temperature
(1000 K). It appears that the NNP600 allows a better description of the interlayer space during
NPT simulations as compared to NNP400. Comparing the two NNPs, when looking at the
lattice angles computed after NPT MD, NNP400 reproduces DFT values more accurately than
NNP600. The elastic properties of the pyrophyllite at 0 GPa predicted by the developed NNPs
conform to other theoretical studies as well as experimental results. Other properties such
as exfoliation energy and vibrational density of state are also rather accurately described.
These results are very encouraging, as these are the first NNPs allowing the description of
clay layers held together only by van der Waals interactions. The obtained dataset and
NNPS parameters are made public and can be used freely. This study will be continued
by including the descritpion of edges, tetrahedral and ocatahedral substitutions as well as
hydrated cations.

Abstract: In this study, a high dimensional neural network potential for the smectite pyro- phyllite clay has been developped from DFT data including correction for dispersion interactions. The dataset has been built from the adaptive learning approach, resulting in a diverse and very concise set of selected structures comprising only representative ones. Two NNP datasets have been constituted from sets of energies and forces com- puted at two different levels of DFT accuracy. Validation tests show very good accuracy for the computed energies and forces of various systems differing by their size and simu- lation conditions. The developed potentials are able to reproduce structural parameters with excellent agreement with DFT values as well as experimental data, and are the first NNPS able to reproduce clay layers’ properties held together via van der Waals interactions. The NNP constructed from data of higher DFT level show better results for extreme condition simulations. In addition, elastic properties, exfoliation energies and vibrational density of state are also well reproduced showing better performances than standard force fields at a fraction of DFT computation time.
